en_segments: If the mistaken judge was an expert of the beit din, etc. Sema, seif katan 20, understands this to mean one who is both learned and capable of independent reasoning. He explains that Rambam adds the words "of the beit din" because in Rambam's terminology a plain "expert" can sometimes mean one who is learned but not fully capable of analysis. According to Sema, above in seif 2, where an accepted expert who errs in judicial discretion is exempt if the loss cannot be reversed, even one who is merely learned but not fully analytical could qualify. Shach, seif katan 22, correctly rejects this. No authority grants the legal status of an expert judge to one who is learned but incapable of reasoned adjudication. For all relevant rules the judge must be a complete expert, both learned and capable of independent reasoning. The phrase "expert of the beit din" in Rambam is therefore either a textual corruption, an explanatory gloss that entered the text, or a scribal expansion. It does not create a lower category of expertise. That is correct as practical law. A separate issue concerns one who is learned but not fully capable of independent reasoning and who received authorization from the Exilarch. Shach cites Rambam's Commentary to the Mishnah and other authorities that such authorization does not help. Without acceptance by the litigants, his judgment has no validity. Baal HaMaor likewise holds so. Tur and Rosh disagree and hold that authorization can be effective for one who is learned even if not fully reasoned. Mordechai in Perek Echad Dinei Mamonot lists a case of one who is learned but not fully reasoned, whom the litigants accepted or who obtained authorization from the Exilarch. Or if he was not an expert, but they accepted him, etc. Here Baal HaMaor and Ramban disagree. Baal HaMaor holds that acceptance helps where the judge is learned but not fully expert. It does not help a person who has no Torah learning at all. Such a person is an asherah, an unfit object, and acceptance cannot transform him into a judge. Ramban disagrees. He asks: why should this differ from the Mishnah's case where the parties accept three cattle herders? R. Yonah explains that their dispute depends upon the law above in siman 22 concerning acceptance where there are two independent defects. A person who is both a single judge and wholly unlearned has two defects. If so, according to Rama above, who rules that ordinary acceptance does not cure two defects without a kinyan, the same should apply here. But this explanation is not necessary. A single recognized expert is permitted to judge alone. Therefore the numerical fact that there is only one judge is not inherently a defect in itself. The only true defect here is lack of expertise. Shach himself uses similar reasoning above in siman 22 concerning an expert judge who is also a relative. See what I wrote there. More fundamentally, the case of three cattle herders is conceptually different. When the parties accept cattle herders, they are obviously not asking them to rule according to precise Torah law. These men do not know Torah law. The acceptance means: "Decide according to your own judgment and assessment, and we accept that outcome." That kind of arbitration can be binding after final judgment because the parties knowingly chose lay decision-makers. If he personally took and gave, etc. It appears that this does not require the judge himself physically to take from one litigant and hand the property to the other. If, in a case where the law authorizes seizure of assets from one who refuses to comply with a judgment, the beit din's agent takes the defendant's property at the judge's direction and gives it to the plaintiff in accordance with the ruling, that too is considered "the judge took and gave." The court agent acts by the judge's command and as his agent. Throughout Torah law, a person's agent is like himself. There is therefore no difference between the judge carrying out the transfer personally and the beit din's agent doing so on his instructions. Rif's exclusion applies only where the litigant did not resist at all and voluntarily paid merely because of the judge's ruling. In that case Rif treats the judge's role as indirect causation, and because the judge is exempt from payment, the judgment can be reversed. But where the judge orders the beit din's agent to descend upon the litigant's assets, seize them forcibly, and transfer them to the opposing party, this is fully within the category of taking and giving. This also resolves Nimukei Yosef's difficulty against Rif. The Gemara says that one who wishes to judge and, if he errs, not be required to pay, should obtain authorization from the Exilarch. Nimukei Yosef asks: why is authorization needed? The judge could simply avoid personally taking and giving. That would be strained if "taking and giving" required the judge's own hands. Why should a judge ordinarily undertake such a burdensome act? But according to what I have explained, the matter is straightforward. The judgment is reversed. Rosh writes that even if the opposing litigant is present and has sufficient property to repay what he received improperly, the judge remains exempt and what the judge wrongfully transferred can nevertheless be recovered through reversal of the judgment. The rule is "what he did is done" only in the category where the law leaves the result standing. Rosh rejects Baal HaItur's citation in the name of Rav Hai Gaon. Rav Hai is reported to hold that where a single nonexpert judge was accepted by the parties, so long as it remains possible to recover the property from the litigant who received it, the court recovers from that litigant even if the judge personally took and gave. Only where recovery from the litigant is impossible does the judge become liable for the personal transfer. Rosh understood Rav Hai as speaking about an error in judicial discretion. On that reading one would have to say that in this responsum Rav Hai followed Rif and Rav Chisda: without personal taking and giving the judgment is reversed. If the judge personally transferred the property, the judgment ordinarily stands and the judge pays only when recovery from the recipient is impossible.
